questions.question: Explain the difference between theoretical probability and relative frequency, and give one situation where each is the right engine.
questions.expected_answer: Theoretical probability counts what could happen: when all outcomes are equally likely, P(E) = n(E)/n(S) — right for fair spinners, coins, dice and shaken bags. Relative frequency counts what did happen: occurrences divided by trials — right for lopsided or unpredictable things like a drawing pin, a bottle top or the weather, where outcomes are not equally likely and only data can estimate the probability.

questions.question: A bag holds 4 yellow, 5 purple and 3 orange marbles. A learner says P(purple) = 1/3 'because purple is one colour out of three'. Correct the reasoning and give the right answer.
questions.expected_answer: The equally likely outcomes are the twelve individual marbles, not the three colours — purple has five chances in the draw while orange has only three. So the denominator is n(S) = 12 and P(purple) = 5/12. Count things, never types.

questions.question: Why does a fair coin showing 33 heads in 60 tosses raise no suspicion, while a coin showing 2 100 heads in 3 000 tosses does? Use the idea of relative frequency settling.
questions.expected_answer: Relative frequency wobbles in small samples and settles toward the true value as trials increase. 33/60 = 0,55 is normal short-run wobble around the theoretical 0,5. But over 3 000 tosses the estimate should have settled very close to 0,5; a settled value of 0,7 sits far from theory with a large sample behind it, which is strong evidence the coin is weighted.
